title: Minimally invasive assembly of functional tissue inside the body

concept.text: The proposed innovation is to build functional tissue directly at an internal injury site using minimally invasive delivery and precise control over where cells and supportive materials assemble. Instead of preparing a complete graft elsewhere and then implanting it, clinicians would deliver suitable materials into the body and organize them locally into a repair construct. The intended endpoint is viable tissue that receives an adequate blood supply, integrates with its surroundings and performs the required biological function.

One demonstrated enabling approach is imaging-guided deep tissue in vivo sound printing, developed by Davoodi and colleagues. Bioinks are delivered through injection or catheters, and focused ultrasound cross-links biomaterials at selected internal locations under imaging guidance. This establishes a way to fabricate material structures inside living animals. Turning such structures into durable, functional replacement tissue remains the larger proposed breakthrough.

significance.text: Successful assembly at an injury site could change where and how tissue repair is performed. For suitable injuries, it could remove the need to manufacture and surgically implant a complete graft, allowing repair materials to be delivered and shaped locally. The animal fabrication work provides a technical basis for this possibility, but it does not establish that the resulting treatment would restore human tissue function or reduce the overall burden of care.

Conditional synthesis: If local assembly also achieved reliable blood supply, integration and durable performance, it could expand the injuries amenable to repair and reduce dependence on separately manufactured grafts for some applications. These possibilities depend on the tissue, injury and treatment workflow. Printing or solidifying a biomaterial is only one part of tissue replacement; precision of fabrication alone does not establish biological function, clinical benefit or the ability to construct an entire organ.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unsolved capability is to place and organize living cells and supportive material at clinically meaningful depth and scale while preserving viability and obtaining useful tissue function. The supplied study identifies scale and spatial resolution as fabrication challenges and reports short-term viability of printed cells. Those results do not establish that a sufficiently large repair construct can remain viable, become vascularized, integrate with the host and sustain tissue-specific performance.

Engineering synthesis: A practical system must coordinate material delivery, imaging, assembly and biological maturation within an existing tissue environment. Concrete barriers include controlling the location and extent of cross-linking, maintaining the intended distribution of cells and materials, and achieving adequate scale without sacrificing precision or viability. At the biological level, the construct must acquire sufficient blood supply and connect appropriately to surrounding tissue. The required organization and connections will differ by target tissue, so a successful fabrication method cannot by itself resolve every repair application.

current_state.text: In “Imaging-guided deep tissue in vivo sound printing,” published on 8 May 2025, Elham Davoodi and colleagues reported imaging-guided focused-ultrasound cross-linking of biomaterials in living animals. The main article describes printing near mouse bladder tumors and deep within rabbit leg muscles. These are demonstrations of internal fabrication in animal settings; the mouse experiment should not be described as established repair of a bladder injury. The work does not demonstrate a complete vascularized human organ or substantial functional tissue repair in humans.

The article also reports that printed cells exhibited high viability for seven days after printing. This supports short-term compatibility of the printing process with living cells within the reported experiments. It does not establish long-term survival, functional vascularization, host integration or durable repair, and the supplied review does not establish that this cell-viability result was measured within the same in vivo animal constructs.

The supplied review had the complete eight-page main article, with no reported text-extraction truncation. Supplementary methods, figures and movies were absent, and figure images were not independently inspected. The experimental account therefore rests on the article's explicit prose as assessed in that review, without independent examination of the supplementary evidence or visual results.

Evidence limitation: The supplied record establishes a dated May 2025 result, but contains no freshness-search findings establishing whether later work changed the field by 1 November 2026. It therefore supports this account of the documented experiment, rather than a comprehensive claim about the latest state of the field. The absence of that update does not invalidate the reported animal fabrication result.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: Controlled studies should show that minimally invasive assembly inside the body reproducibly repairs substantial injury in at least one human tissue, with durable tissue-specific function and either superior outcomes or a material reduction in treatment burden relative to the appropriate existing treatment. A protocol would need to define the injury, comparator, functional endpoints, follow-up duration and clinically meaningful benefit in advance. These are proposed operational criteria, not established consensus standards or results already achieved.
completion_criteria.label: In-body assembly reproducibly restores durable human tissue function with comparative benefit

completion_criteria.text: Proposed supporting evidence: Evaluation should establish the construct's location and organization, viability, adequate blood supply, host integration and appropriate function over the specified follow-up period. It should also assess unintended effects of delivery and assembly, the need for additional procedures, and whether any reduction in implantation burden persists across the full course of treatment. Reproduction across patients and, where feasible, independent teams would make the result more convincing than an isolated successful case.
completion_criteria.label: Construct performance and full treatment burden are assessed throughout follow-up

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: Demonstrations should report the tissue types, injury sizes, anatomical depths, material and cell formulations, and patient conditions for which the method works. Success in one tissue would establish a consequential capability within that scope. Broader applicability would require separate demonstrations, and finite testing would establish demonstrated breadth rather than literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Demonstrated tissue repair scope and practical boundaries are reported

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: BME-01, “Manufacturing transplantable human organs on demand,” overlaps in the need to fabricate organized, viable tissue. BME-17 focuses on delivery and assembly inside the body, whereas BME-01's title centers on producing transplantable organs. A locally assembled repair construct could advance BME-17 without constituting a complete transplantable organ. Conversely, manufacturing an organ for transplantation would not by itself demonstrate minimally invasive assembly at an internal injury site.

Roster-based comparison: BME-11, “Controlled regeneration of complex organs in the adult body,” shares the goal of restoring tissue within an adult patient. BME-17 specifically concerns placing and organizing cells and supportive materials at the site of repair; BME-11's title describes the broader biological outcome of controlled organ regeneration. The approaches could overlap if an assembled construct helps direct regeneration, but successful local fabrication and successful complex-organ regeneration remain distinct achievements.

Roster-based comparison: BME-15, “Accessible deep-body molecular imaging,” and BME-16, “Long-lived tissue-integrated interfaces for implants,” describe potentially relevant enabling or adjacent capabilities. Imaging may help guide assembly, but guidance does not necessarily require molecular imaging or establish BME-15's accessibility goal. Durable contact with host tissue is relevant to BME-17, but a tissue repair construct does not automatically constitute the implant interface envisioned by BME-16. These comparisons use the supplied titles; full definitions of the other entries were not provided, so their exact boundaries remain provisional.

change_log.change: Preserved BME-17's identity and expanded the explanation of minimally invasive delivery, imaging guidance and local assembly.
change_log.reason: The research and review jointly identify where and how fabrication occurs as the concept's distinguishing contribution.

change_log.change: Dated the reported experiment to 8 May 2025 and replaced the general mouse bladder-lesion description with the specific bladder-tumor context.
change_log.reason: The review supports that experimental setting and does not establish bladder-injury repair.

change_log.change: Integrated the seven-day printed-cell viability result while separating it from long-term survival and in vivo functional repair.
change_log.reason: The quantitative finding supports short-term viability, with insufficient supplied detail to equate it with durable integrated tissue.

change_log.change: Separated demonstrated biomaterial fabrication from the proposed achievement of vascularized, integrated, functional tissue.
change_log.reason: The enabling method does not itself establish human repair or complete-organ fabrication.

change_log.change: Expanded completion criteria into explicitly proposed comparative, reproducibility and practical-scope demonstrations.
change_log.reason: The candidate's endpoint needs operational definitions and should not be presented as an established standard or universal capability.

change_log.change: Preserved article-access limitations and the absence of a freshness assessment.
change_log.reason: The complete main text was available to the review, but supplementary evidence, independent figure inspection and later-field coverage were not.

change_log.change: Used the supplied roster titles to explain overlaps and distinctions, while retaining uncertainty about full entry boundaries.
change_log.reason: The roster permits title-level comparisons with BME-01 and BME-11, but does not supply their complete definitions.

unresolved_issues: The supplied record does not establish whether developments after May 2025 changed the field by 1 November 2026.
Supplementary methods, figures and movies were unavailable to the supplied review, and figure images were not independently inspected.
The supplied review does not resolve the experimental context of the seven-day cell-viability result sufficiently to attribute it to the reported in vivo constructs.
A clinical protocol must define substantial injury, durability, meaningful treatment-burden reduction, comparators and acceptable adverse effects for a specific tissue.
The exact boundaries with other roster entries require their full definitions; the comparisons here are limited to supplied titles.

brief.title: Building working tissue inside the body
possible: People with internal injuries could have replacement tissue built where it is needed. Doctors would deliver living cells and supporting materials through injections or thin tubes, then organize them at the injury site. The tissue would receive blood, connect with its surroundings and perform the damaged tissue’s job.
why: For suitable injuries, this could replace the need to make a complete tissue graft elsewhere and surgically implant it. Building tissue locally could expand the injuries doctors can repair and reduce the burden of treatment.

sources.who: Elham Davoodi, Wei Gao and colleagues
sources.showed: The team used focused ultrasound, which concentrates sound waves, to solidify supporting materials at selected sites inside living animals. They formed structures near mouse bladder tumors and within rabbit leg muscles.
sources.quote:
we demonstrated in vivo printing within the bladders and
muscles of live animals
sources.cited_for: Sound waves can control where injected materials form structures inside living animals.
sources.not_established: The work did not establish lasting repair by living tissue with a blood supply and connections to its surroundings.

sources.who: Anna Urciuolo, Nicola Elvassore and colleagues
sources.showed: The team used laser light to shape injected materials inside living mice. Donor cells formed new muscle fibres that connected with the host’s functioning network of blood vessels.
sources.quote:
supports 
the generation of newly formed myofibre bundles that are integrated 
with the functional vascular network of the host.
sources.cited_for: Local assembly can support new muscle formation and connections to a functioning blood supply in mice.
sources.not_established: New muscle fibres in mice do not establish durable recovery of human tissue function or an advantage over existing treatment.

sources.showed: The team delivered a tiny robot through a viewing tube and guided it with a magnetic field to arrange cells inside inflamed mouse colons. Some patterned cells remained detectable after nine days.
sources.quote: Furthermore, as a proof-of-concept, cell patterning was performed inside the colon of mice with colitis.
sources.cited_for: A tiny robot can place cells in controlled patterns at damaged sites inside living mice.
sources.not_established: Cell placement and short-term survival do not establish working replacement tissue or lasting repair.

shown: Animal studies have demonstrated both internal fabrication and some biological assembly. Davoodi and colleagues formed material structures using sound waves. Urciuolo and colleagues went further biologically: donor cells formed new muscle fibres connected to functioning blood vessels in mice.

Yamazoe and colleagues arranged cells inside damaged mouse colons with a magnetically guided robot. These results establish parts of the process; durable restoration of substantial human tissue injury remains undemonstrated.
missing: Assembly must work at useful depths and sizes while preserving cell survival and the intended arrangement of cells and materials.
A substantial repair must maintain its blood supply, connect with surrounding tissue and perform its required job over time.
Human studies must demonstrate repeatable, lasting repair and better outcomes or a meaningful reduction in the full burden of treatment.

milestones.label: Lasting human tissue repair with comparative benefit
milestones.explanation: Controlled human studies would have to show repeatable, lasting repair with better outcomes or meaningfully less treatment burden than existing care. This would establish a useful treatment for a defined injury.

milestones.label: Sustained tissue performance and full treatment burden measured
milestones.explanation: Follow-up would have to track tissue organization, survival, blood supply, integration, function, unintended effects and extra procedures across patients. This would establish whether repair and reduced treatment burden persist.

milestones.label: The range and limits of successful repair established
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to identify which tissues, injury sizes, depths, materials, cells and patient conditions support successful repair. This would define where the treatment works and where separate demonstrations remain necessary.

uncertain: The required cell organization and connections differ by tissue, so success in one tissue may not carry over to another.
Each treatment needs clear standards for substantial injury, lasting function, meaningful benefit and acceptable unintended effects.
